newsitem.title: USA: Round-the-world balloonist off Iberian coast.
newsitem.headline: Round-the-world balloonist off Iberian coast.

text.p: Adventurer Steve Fossett passed just south of the Spanish-Portugese border on Thursday, completing his Atlantic crossing in a bid to become the first to circle the world nonstop in a balloon.
But his expedition said the 52-year-old American might have to scrap his attempt for the record over North Africa if he does not get permission to cross Libya.

At 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT) his craft was 45 miles (72.42 km) due south of the Iberian border point and had been sighted visually by an air traffic control centre in Portugal, his expedition's headquarters in Chicago said.
He was being pushed along at speeds up to 90 miles (144 km) per hour by winter jetstreams as he entered the Mediterranean region.
Unresolved was the question of whether he would receive clearance to pass over Libya, which he could reach on Saturday unless he can find wind currents that will allow him to skirt that country.
The expedition said on Thursday if he could not find another route and reached Libya without word or clearance "he will probably have to put the craft down" and end his quest for the record.

Fossett already holds the record for the longest solo manned balloon flight -- 5,435.8 miles (8,747 km) on a voyage from South Korea to Canada -- a mark that he would better on this voyage over southeast Algeria, the expedition said, before he reached Libya.

British Tycoon Richard Branson and Swiss pilot Jean Piccard, who failed in separate missions this month to capture the record Fossett was seeking, said they would take to the air in Branson's Citation, a small corporate jet, to circle the silver "Solo Spirit" balloon as a welcome in the Gibraltar area.
It was not clear whether the rendezvous would take place at night or after daybreak on Friday.
"Everything is going just great," a spokesman for the expedition said.

Bo Kemper, chief spokesman for the record-setting solo attempt, said Branson was also attempting to intercede with the Libyan government on Fossett's behalf, and the expedition's Internet site carried an appeal on Thursday for letters to President Bill Clinton to try to resolve the problem.

Permission had neither been given nor denied "and we have meteorologists trying to figure out how to go under or below (south of Libya)," Kemper said. "We have overflight permission from Niger, Chad and Sudan, Algeria and Morocco."

The Colorado-based commodities broker lifted off from St. Louis late on Monday in pursuit of one of manned flight's oldest goals but was forced to take a more southerly path than originally planned after he could not win permission from Russia to cross that country on a northern trans-European route.
The expedition said problems including language barriers between Fossett and Russian air traffic controllers as well as stormy weather farther north prompted the turn southward.
After crossing North Africa he hoped to traverse Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, China, Mongolia, China again, perhaps Korea and then head across the Pacific, it said.

He was able to sleep in his unpressurized 6-1/2 by four foot (two by 1.3 metre) yellow capsule, which had an alarm to rouse him should the balloon suddenly change altitude. The enclosed gondola is 5-1/2 feet (1.7 metres) high.
The trip could take up to 18 days.

Piccard and Wim Verstraeten wound up in the Mediterranean on Sunday six hours after taking off from the Swiss Alps in pursuit of the record. Branson and two crew members brought their Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria last week less than a day after taking off from Morocco.
